title: Reserved pool dimensioning workshop — Aurora POC notes
summary: Working notes from the Aurora customer workshop on reserved-pool dimensioning and scale policies. Captures measured throughput heuristics, suggested pool composition, a conservative cost run, and short-term mitigations for bursty traffic patterns.
notes:
Context and ask:
- Customer: Aurora (SaaS analytics). Wants predictable latency for interactive features (query assistant) with fixed monthly budget and compliance constraints (no multi-tenant shared hosts).
- Ask: propose a reserved inference pool design (customer-managed fleet via Redwood Private or Dedicated-like reserved pool) that meets p95 latency <= 600ms for interactive prompts and supports 3x burst capacity for marketing events.

Observed workload profile (from their telemetry + sample traces):
- Baseline steady traffic: 12 requests/sec (avg) during business hours.
- Typical spike pattern: short spikes up to 80 req/sec for 3-10 minutes (promotional batch).
- Avg prompt size: 140 input tokens + 40 generated tokens (total 180 tokens) for assistant flows.
- 70% of requests are short (<=50 gen tokens), 20% medium (50-200), 10% long (>200).

Model options considered (customer preference: open models + quantized variants):
- rwd-7B-q4 (fast, cheaper) — target p95 single-request latency friendly for short prompts
- rwd-13B-q8 (higher quality, ~1.6x cost/latency of 7B) — suggested for fallback for enterprise tier users
- rwd-7B-int8 (if available) — experimental; lower latency but less stable in evals

Performance heuristics and steady-state math (conservative):
- Measured token generation throughput per A100-like instance when running rwd-7B-q4: ~1,200 tokens/sec (observed during internal benching with batching). For planning we use 1,000 tokens/sec to include CPU/IO overhead and tail variability.
- Effective tokens/request (avg): 180 => 1 req consumes ~0.18s of pure generation time at 1,000 tps; but end-to-end with attention/overheads, we budget 0.35s per request on rwd-7B-q4. => approx 2.85 req/sec capacity per GPU instance.
- Steady compute capacity needed for 12 req/sec: 12 / 2.85 = 4.2 => round up to 5 reserved instances for baseline.

Burst sizing (safety and graceful degradation):
- Target: absorb 3x baseline (36 req/sec) without queueing beyond 1s p95. 36 / 2.85 = 12.6 => 13 instances.
- To avoid paying for 13 instances 24/7, propose a two-tier pool:
  - Primary reserved pool: 6 instances (covers baseline + overhead; modest buffer)
  - Fast-burst standby: 8 pre-warmed instances in a low-cost standby pool that can be instantly promoted (warm caches, KV preloaded). Promotion mechanism: traffic-based policy + pre-warm signal from Redwood control plane. Effective committed pool = 14 (6 active, 8 standby) but only 6 billed as hot in steady-state if standby in a paused/low-power billing mode is supported. If customer needs strict reserved billing, then commit to 13 active instances with scheduling windows.

Autoscale / promote policy (policy sketch):
- Scale up trigger: sustained incoming RPS > baseline_threshold for 15s OR queued requests > 10 for 5s.
- Promotion order: standby pre-warmed rwd-7B-q4 instances -> spin up additional rwd-7B-q4 if standby exhausted -> degrade lower-priority requests to rwd-7B-q8 fallback (slower but higher quality) only when explicit per-route rules allow it.
- Scale down: idle 10m with CPU and GPU utilization < 8% and queue empty -> demote to standby. Avoid scale-down during predictable traffic windows (marketing).

Quality vs cost trade: fallback and graceful degradation
- For enterprise users (10% of traffic), route to rwd-13B-q8 pools pinned to above baseline (no fallback).
- For public users, when capacity constrained, serve with rwd-7B-q4 with conservative temperature / max_tokens reduction to maintain latency SLO while reducing per-request compute. This lowers avg tokens per request from 180 to ~140 during pressure windows (reduces compute need ~22%).

Cost sketch (conservative, monthly):
- Pricing assumptions (on-demand list): A100-equivalent reserved instance = $3.5/hr, A10G-equivalent = $1.9/hr. We plan on A100-equivalent for high-memory 13B runs and A10G for 7B quantized. For simplicity assume mix below.
- Baseline plan (recommended committed): 6 x A10G (active) + 8 x A10G (standby/prewarmed) + 2 x A100 (pinned for enterprise 13B) => active billing model depends on customer contract. Worst-case always-on billing: (6+8)*A10G + 2*A100 = 14*1.9 + 2*3.5 = $26.6/hr + $7.0/hr = $33.6/hr => ~$24,192/month (730h).
- Committed discounts: with 30% commit discount expected monthly ~ $16,935. Practical recommended sign: commit to 6 always-on A10G + 2 always-on A100 and 8 standby charged only when promoted => estimated steady monthly owners cost ~ $10,500 - $14,000 depending on standby billing model.
- Note: network, storage, license, and Redwood platform fee (15%) on top of raw infra. Add buffer +20% for total customer budget planning.

Operational runbooks / engineering notes:
- Pre-warm recipe: start inference container, load model weights into GPU memory, populate KV/prefix cache with top-200 prompts extracted from recent usage (script provided in linked GitHub PR). This reduces first-requests tail significantly.
- Health checks: expose token-level latency histograms; p95 and p99 alerts when >600ms and >1.25s respectively.
- Fallback circuit: if model GPU memory pressure >90% or instance OOM errors observed, immediately remove instance from routing and trigger autoscaler to promote standby.

Risks and unknowns:
- Benchmark variance: our 1,000 tps conservative assumption for rwd-7B-q4 needs tuning to Aurora’s input length distribution and exact quantization pipeline. Request a 24-hour trace + small on-customer benchmark (10k synthetic requests) to validate.
- Standby billing semantics differ by cloud provider. Confirm whether pre-warmed paused instances incur full billing or a reduced rate (some clouds charge for reserved capacity even if VM in stopped state).
- SLO enforcement across regions: Aurora expects EU and US coverage; replicate pool across two regions and use smart routing to keep cross-region latency low (adds +~40% infra cost).

Quick wins (next 2 weeks):
- Run a focused bench with Aurora sample trace for rwd-7B-q4 and rwd-13B-q8 (Jenkins job / GitHub action).
- Prototype standby-to-active promotion script and validate warm-cache hit rate improvement.
- Draft customer-friendly cost sheet showing three buy profiles: minimal (baseline), burst-ready (two-tier with standby), and enterprise-fixed (always-on heavy).

Notes on metrics we should collect during PoC:
- per-request breakdown: input tokens, generated tokens, time in queue, GPU utilization sampled every 1s, cold-start duration, cache hit rate for prefix/KV.
- business metrics mapping: convert degraded-response rate -> estimated percent of support tickets and query completion rate.

Reference snippets and useful links: see linked_artifacts above for bench PR and Confluence overview. Also consult the thrifted runbook: SE-ops/warmup-playbook (internal).

End of notes.
